detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the standard West Route. The true (south) summit has one short mantle move onto a block; otherwise it's a walk.
pro_needs: No trad gear is placed on the standard route - it is a scree/talus/grass walk-up with one short 3rd-class move near the true summit. A rope/harness/rack is only relevant if linking into one of the technical buttress routes (Middle Finger Buttress, Finger of Fatwa, Pilgrimage to Mecca) on the same peak.
what_to_bring: ice axe and possibly crampons for lingering snow before ~mid-July
sun protection - long exposed alpine walk
map/GPS - open terrain with braided boot paths
beta: From Upper Cathedral Lake, follow a boot path southeast onto the west ridge/basin, then hike scree and grassy slopes northeasterly into a basin around 8,000 ft before a final walk to the summit. Alternatively, from the Cathedral Peak side a gully/col can be used to reach the same upper basin. The route is Class 2 throughout, with brief Class 3 sections depending on line choice; no rope or technical gear is used by most parties. Frequently combined with Cathedral Peak (Class 3, about one mile away) on the same trip.

detailed_rack: Minimal. A short rope, a few nuts and cams to 3 inches for the chimney and any belays you decide to build, and half a dozen long runners for slinging chockstones and horns. A rappel device and a couple of spare slings and rap rings to replace or back up the fixed anchor near the top. Helmets throughout — the couloir funnels everything the upper mountain sheds.
pro_needs: The route is Class 3, so most parties move unroped over most of it, but the chockstone chimney and the upper friction slab are the two places where a rope is worth having, and the slab in particular offers very little to place — the large flake used as a handrail is the main feature. Slinging chockstones in the couloir gives the most reliable anchors on this rock.
what_to_bring: Helmet (critical given the documented rockfall accident here)
Rope/rappel device if descending past the chockstone
ice axe and crampons — early in the season, since this aspect stays snow-filled
beta: The Northwest Couloir climbs to a chockstone in the upper gully; parties commonly rappel or downclimb past the chockstone. Some parties descend it back toward Peggy's Pond, but the standard descent from the summit is the Southwest Face. The couloir holds notably loose, fractured rock.

detailed_rack: Deliberately light. A picket and a rope are suggested - a 50m is preferred over a 30m - and slung trees provide the occasional belay on the flanks. Rock protection is minimal during peak season, so do not plan a rack around it: bring a few slings and a couple of nuts if you want them; most of this route is climbed with the axe and your feet. A second tool is worth considering for the steepest upper section even though the route is graded as snow rather than ice.
pro_needs: Minimal. A picket, a few slings for trees, and the acceptance that much of the 70-degree upper gully is effectively unprotected.
what_to_bring: Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass for the PCT North trailhead
Insulated layers and shell - half the gully never sees sun
Sunglasses and sunscreen for the sunlit half
Map/GPS track for both the Commonwealth and Cave Ridge descents
beta: A Grade II snow climb and the steepest of Guye's gully lines. The angle runs about 45 degrees for the first few hundred feet, then gets progressively steeper the higher you go, reaching roughly 70 degrees near the top. It finishes at the ridge separating the true and false summits. About half the gully sits in shade and half in sun, which the first-ascent party found gave pretty solid snow under the surface - a useful characteristic that also means conditions can differ markedly between the two halves on a warm day. Protection is minimal: an ice axe is mandatory and crampons are required, a picket and rope are suggested (a 50m is preferred over a 30m), rock protection is scarce in peak season, and slung trees provide occasional belays. This is a route where good snow makes it straightforward and bad snow makes it seriously exposed.

detailed_rack: A medium alpine rock rack — small-to-mid cams and a set of nuts — plus 8-10 shoulder-length runners for the long, wandering pitches. Matches the published route description.
pro_needs: Standard alpine rock protection to about 2-3 inches with 8-10 runners to manage rope drag on the long, wandering pitches. The crux final pitch (5.8- PG13) protects only moderately well. Helmet and a single ice axe for the shared glacier approach.
rack: 1 snow picket + ice axe for approach
what_to_bring: bivy/camping gear for a 2-3 day trip
approach shoes/boots suited to brush and slab
extra layers for exposed ridge climbing
beta: Parties reach the east end of the Terror Glacier via the same Terror Basin approach as the West Ridge, then climb roughly six pitches of alpine rock (up to 5.8-, rated PG13) up the southwest ridge/face to the summit. There is no pitch-by-pitch description; most parties climb it fully roped rather than scrambled.

detailed_rack: Helmets are essential due to loose Olympic basalt and rockfall hazard.
pro_needs: Rock scrambling experience, comfortable with exposure, navigation skills (map, compass, GPS). Helmets recommended due to rockfall hazard and loose rock common to Olympic basalt.
what_to_bring: 10 essentials (map, compass, sunscreen, first aid, knife, fire starter, shelter, extra clothes, extra food, extra water)
Backpack (20-25L for day hike, 40L+ for overnight)
ice axe — recommended June-July when snow and ice patches are common
trekking poles — steep descent on Putvin Trail
beta: From Hamma Hamma River Road, hike the steep Putvin Trail (FST 813) through Olympic National Forest gaining nearly 3,000 feet in less than 4 miles. Emerge in an alpine basin at Lake of the Angels (~4,900 feet), then traverse along the base of the cliffs short of St. Peter's Gate to a notch in the West Ridge, then scramble Class 3 up the ridge with some exposed class 4 moves to reach the South Peak summit.

detailed_rack: A light alpine rack suffices for 5.6 ridge climbing on granodiorite: a single set of cams roughly from small to #2 Camalot, a set of nuts, a good number of long slings for the ridge's horns and blocks, and a 60 m rope, which also covers the 25 m descent rappel. Bring a cordelette and some spare tat for building or backing up belays and the rappel anchor. Helmets throughout — the gully and the talus descent are loose.
pro_needs: Minimal and mostly slung. The sharp ridge takes long slings over horns and blocks more than it takes cam placements, so weight the rack toward runners. A single set of cams and nuts covers the occasional crack. The only place where protection genuinely matters is the summit block itself, which is a short but seriously exposed V1 boulder problem — most parties belay it rather than solo it.
rack: Light trad rack (small-to-medium cams and nuts)
Single 60 m rope (covers the ~25 m descent rappel)
what_to_bring: Helmet — the gully and the talus descent are loose
Approach shoes or light boots for the trail, gully and talus
2-3 L water capacity and a filter; Colchuck Lake is the last reliable water
Wind shell and warm layer for an exposed northwest ridge
Ice axe and microspikes before mid-July
Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass
beta: The Northwest Ridge is the moderate line on Colchuck Balanced Rock and the route of choice for parties who want the summit rather than the west face's hard free climbing. The line gains an obvious gully from Colchuck Lake to the notch above Jabberwocky Tower, then third-class terrain leading to the ridge proper, followed by the sharp ridge at 5.6 to the summit. Total gain from the Stuart Lake Trailhead to the summit is about 4,760 ft, and a relaxed car-to-car time is roughly 12 hours. The final obstacle is the balanced summit block itself, a short boulder problem that most parties protect. Descent from the summit was a single 25 m rappel off an anchor down the east side, then scrambling talus around to the south saddle and back past Jabberwocky Tower to Colchuck Lake. The rock is granodiorite. The peak's first ascent was made in 1958 by Gene Prater and Thomas Quin, though not necessarily by this line.

detailed_rack: No rack is needed for the scrambling. What parties actually carry for this route is a short rope (30–40 m is plenty, though most bring the 60 m they have anyway), harnesses for everyone, a few slings and prusik cord to rig a handline over the step-across, and a couple of slings/nuts to build an anchor on either side of the chasm. Helmets for the loose blocks lower down.
pro_needs: Essentially none on the scrambling, which is protected by good judgement rather than gear. The only place people want protection is the step-across chasm, where an anchor built from slung blocks plus a fixed handline and prusiks is the standard rig. Parties describe using a rope and harnesses specifically for this one move.
what_to_bring: Free self-issue Pasayten wilderness permit (at the trailhead)
Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass
Offline maps downloaded before the drive
Head net and repellent for July–mid-August mosquitoes
Water filter — Upper Cathedral Lake is reliable year-round water
Trekking poles for the sandy slopes and the 17+ mile approach
beta: Also referred to as the West Ridge or the southwest slope, and universally described as the easy way up and the route of choice for descending after climbing the Southeast or North faces. From Upper Cathedral Lake (7,380 ft) take the trail 0.6 miles nearly to Cathedral Pass (7,600 ft), leave it, and climb easy sandy terrain for several hundred vertical feet. Ducks and cairns then lead over Class 2-3 granite outcrops, blocks and slabs — solid, coarsely crystalline rock with occasional spots where a friction hoist gets you over a block — to a hidden cleft running parallel to and just below the west ridge crest. There are two minor Class 3+ steps, and the summit chasm is crossed twice; the harder of the two step-acrosses is the Class 4 move. The chasm that cleaves the summit rocks into north and south sections is the crux: step onto a large chockstone jammed in the slot and mantle onto a bulge on the far side. The climbing is easy; the exposure is dramatic, and most parties carry a rope and harnesses for it, often rigging a handline with prusiks for the return. In early season the chasm is filled with snow, which makes the first of the two step-acrosses easy or trivial; the second never has snow in the hole. Overall the route is Class 3, with that one Class 4 move at the chasm and exposure well beyond the grade.

detailed_rack: A light alpine trad rack: a single set of nuts, cams from small (0.3-0.4) through 3 inches with a piece to 4 inches for the chimney, and a generous supply of single- and double-length runners for slinging horns and blocks — on shattered andesite, slung natural features are often better than a cam in a fractured pocket. A few pitons and a light hammer are not unreasonable on this rock but most parties go without. Helmets are not optional. A single 60m rope is enough for the climb and covers the standard-route rappels.
pro_needs: Protection is where this route earns its seriousness rather than its 5.6 grade. The andesite is fractured and friable, so placements need to be tested and backed up, and camming units in flared, gritty cracks should be treated with suspicion. Sling everything solid you can reach. Long runners keep rope drag down in the chimney and reduce the chance of the rope raking loose blocks onto the belayer.
beta: Documented as a class 5.6 route on the peak's southeast side; no further pitch-by-pitch beta is available.

detailed_rack: There is no established rack for The Chimney, so what follows is standard practice for a single 100 ft pitch of 5.3 on loose alpine sedimentary rock: a single 60 m rope (a 30 m half or tag line technically covers the 100 ft, but a 60 m gives you rappel options), a light single rack of nuts and cams from small to about hand size, a handful of slings for chockstones and horns — chimneys on this rock often protect better with tied-off blocks than with cams — plus a couple of long runners, a cordelette for anchors, and a few pitons only if your party is used to placing them. Helmets are not optional given Olympic rock quality. Bring more slings than you would on granite and expect to build anchors out of whatever is solid rather than what is convenient.
pro_needs: Protection on a short 5.3 Olympic chimney is about finding solid rock, not about having the right cam size. Expect to sling chockstones and horns, to test every placement before weighting it, and to accept some runout where the rock will not take gear. A single light rack plus a generous set of slings is the right tool; a heavy rack mostly buys you weight over the 13.9-mile approach.
what_to_bring: NPS-approved bear canister (required at Enchanted Valley)
Green Trails / CalTopo map and compass
rain shell and warm layer — marine west coast climate, rain any month
camp shoes and dry socks for the rainforest approach
first aid kit sized for a multi-day self-rescue
beta: First climbed in 1970 by Mike Banner and Vern Johnson via class 5.3 climbing, roughly three decades after the peak's summit was first reached (1941) by a non-technical scramble line. The Chimney is the peak's namesake feature: a 100-ft-high chimney-like tower on its west aspect.

detailed_rack: Not documented. Given a 5.9+ grade on an obscure Cascades wall with no recorded fixed gear, a full single rack of cams and nuts, double ropes for a possible retreat, a generous set of slings for blocks and horns, and tat and nuts to leave on a bail anchor would be the conventional preparation. Helmets are not optional on rock this lightly travelled.
pro_needs: Not documented. No bolts, fixed anchors or rappel stations are recorded anywhere on Lichtenberg Mountain, so assume the route is entirely on natural protection and that any anchor you need, you build.
what_to_bring: Offline maps and a downloaded track — there is no reception past US 2
2-3 litres of water; Lake Valhalla is the last source
Insect repellent and head net for July and August at the lake
Northwest Forest Pass for the dashboard
beta: James Nakagami climbed the West Face at 5.9+ with Dan 'Danimal' Capellini and a third partner. The wall sits just above Lake Valhalla; the approach is a short walk from the Smithbrook trailhead of about an hour, and it is an easier walk in than Snow Creek Wall. A grand west face is one of the mountain's three distinct routes, and one party was turned around by the sheer wall before reaching the summit by an easier line, which confirms that this is genuine roped terrain rather than a scramble. Beyond the grade, the location and the approach, the beta is thin: no topo, pitch count, rack list or descent description is available. Anyone going should expect to do their own reconnaissance from Lake Valhalla, and plan for a full trad rack and a walk-off.

detailed_rack: First climbed by Scott Bennett & Blake Herrington in 2012, the route gives ~160m of climbing: a superb fingers-to-thin-hands splitter, then a series of left-leaning roofs topped by hand cracks and jugs. For that terrain, expect doubles in the finger-to-hand range (roughly 0.3-1) for the splitter, plus singles up to #3 for the hand cracks, and a full nut set for the thin sections.
pro_needs: Same Middle Finger Buttress rock as the Left/Right Side routes (sound, well-protected); the roof sections will need extension/slings to manage rope drag more than hard-to-find gear.
what_to_bring: crack gloves recommended for the finger/hand splitter
beta: Pitch 1 climbs a rightward-trending ramp/flake (5.10-ish); pitch 2 is the crux, a ringlock crack, stem corner, and leftward traverse to a belay beneath roofs (5.11c); pitch 3 continues through underclings and jams beneath two roofs into a chimney (5.11b); pitches 4-5 follow hand cracks and blocky terrain trending right, joining the Middle Finger Buttress-Left line on a rib before a scramble to the top.

detailed_rack: Set of stoppers, doubles from BD #0.3 to #2, plus a single #3. Pitch 1 is a full 60m hand-crack/chimney-start pitch at 5.10, pitch 2 a 40m 5.9 dihedral, then 2 (sometimes a 5th) moderate 5.7-5.9 pitches to the top, ~100m+ total.
pro_needs: Sustained crack and dihedral climbing takes cams and stoppers well throughout on sound buttress rock; no fixed gear reported.
what_to_bring: approach shoes for the ~20-mile approach to Upper Cathedral Lake
beta: Begin in a chimney (optional belay at its top), then climb an excellent hand crack (the route's hardest and best pitch), traverse right along a dihedral, and finish on non-sustained 5.7-5.9 terrain to the top, with a possible 5th pitch depending on the exact line chosen.

detailed_rack: The only published protection note for this Grade III, 5.9, 7-pitch route a broad assortment of nuts and cams - no exact sizes/counts are published. The route climbs cracks on the NW side of the buttress, starting on a steep slab with a thin vertical crack, with the crux on pitch 3.
pro_needs: No trip report with a specific gear list was found; treat exact rack sizing as inferred from the thin-crack start plus longer crack pitches - bring a fairly full single rack (nuts + cams roughly finger-to-fist) rather than a minimal one, given 7 pitches of varied crack climbing.
what_to_bring: extra layers/food - 7 pitches makes for a long day
beta: Climbs cracks up the northwest side of the buttress; begins on a steep slab with a thin vertical crack, with the short crux on the 3rd pitch. Historically included a brief C1 aid section, though it may go free at the grade for strong parties.

detailed_rack: The rack is simply a light set of nuts and long slings for this Grade II, 5.5, 5-7 pitch ridge route (pitch count varies with line chosen). Terrain includes sections of loose boulders.
beta: From Cathedral Pass, scramble up to a point where roping up becomes worthwhile, then follow the blunt north ridge through several steps of up-to-5.5 climbing, with route-finding and loose blocks in places, topping out on Amphitheater's broad summit plateau.

detailed_rack: No technical rack needed - this is a hike/scramble with no roped climbing. The route follows the Lower and Upper Maynard Burn Trail from the Maynard Burn (Tyler Peak) trailhead at the end of FR 2870-120, gaining a ridge crest via steep, sometimes faint tread through subalpine meadows and scree/talus to the Baldy summit block. No cams, nuts, or fixed anchors are used or needed by parties climbing the standard route.
pro_needs: None - no protection is placed on the standard route; it is unroped talus/scree hiking and scrambling. Rockfall/loose rock is the main hazard rather than a lack of protection quality, so party spacing and helmets matter more than rack size.
what_to_bring: map and compass or GPS - the boot path fades above treeline and in the summit meadows
trekking poles for the sustained steep grade (route gains ~3,800 ft)
helmet for the loose rock/scree near the summit
ice axe and microspikes if climbing in spring/early season when snow patches remain on the upper slopes/ridge
sun protection - much of the route is above treeline on an exposed ridge
ample water - no water on the route above the ridge crest
beta: From the Maynard Burn (Tyler Peak) trailhead, a steep boot path climbs through rhododendron forest and past an old fire-break (the Maynard Burn track) to reach meadows and then the crest of Gray Wolf Ridge around 2.7 miles (~6,200 ft). Formal trail tread ends shortly after (~2.85 mi), and the final push to the summit is a cross-country scramble over a minor sub-summit and along the open ridge, arriving at Baldy's rocky, view-packed top at 3.6 miles.

detailed_rack: Standard rack to 3 inches with doubles through the smaller-to-mid sizes for the crack systems; the crux pitches take good, solid gear. All of the technical climbing is on solid rock even though the low-5th-class sections are loose.
pro_needs: Gear to 3 inches is sufficient; no wide gear required. Long runners help manage rope drag on the wandering ridge pitches.
beta: Climbs an obvious dihedral system past two trees with webbing to a large terrace, then crack systems and a small dihedral to the crux — two consecutive 5.8 pitches (a finger crack into a splitter hand crack, then a dihedral with bomber finger locks) that can be linked with a 70m rope. Above the crux the route stays on the ridge crest with mostly 3rd-4th class/low-5th scrambling, a short downclimb, and a sandy gully to the summit area.

detailed_rack: Short route — 300ft/3 pitches of blocky Class 5.6 on generally good granite directly below the summit. A single set of nuts plus cams in the 0.4-2in range (with extra pieces in the 0.75-1in range, reported as the most useful crux size) is sufficient; nothing larger is recorded as needed. Bring webbing or a cordelette for backing up the worn rappel anchor above the chockstone on the descent.
pro_needs: Protection is adequate in the crack/corner systems on this face (start in a short left-facing corner and follow cracks up), but rock quality is inconsistent — good overall, with reported loose blocks near the base, so test holds low on the route. The face is wide enough that parties pick their own line.
rack: Webbing/cordelette for the chockstone rappel anchor
what_to_bring: Extra water for the long, exposed south-side approach
beta: Start in the rightmost and larger of two short left-facing corners on the wall base; follow blocky, generally solid rock 'to the summit' with several viable variations up the face. Watch for a few loose blocks low on the route. The grade (5.6) is an old-school rating and climbs sustained, comparable to roughly 5.9-5.10- by modern gym standards.

detailed_rack: A long route (14 pitches of full 60m/200ft length on the 2012 ascent; the 1975 FA logged 22 pitches)
pro_needs: Protection is generally good with cams and nuts on the more solid sections; be selective and test placements on the loose red rock bands noted by repeat ascent parties.
rack: Cams, doubles finger-to-hand sizes (small Aliens most useful), plus #3/#4
what_to_bring: approach shoes for the Hart Lake-to-buttress approach
bivy gear for Hart Lake camp
light rack of slings for horn/block anchors
beta: The 1975 first-ascent party climbed the buttress in 22 pitches over three days using titanium pitons and early Abalakov-style protection; a 2012 ascent using modern gear and 200-ft ropes compressed it to roughly 14 pitches plus 4 belay moves. The route features a major horizontal ledge at half height that is key to the line, a cave belay mid-crux, and three consecutive pitches near 5.10a/b as the technical crux, with much of the remainder in the 5.6-5.9 range. Rock is meta-granitic but includes sections of loose red rock; that party took just under 12 hours from the buttress base to the Southwest Peak.
